list.listitem: There is consistent, good quality evidence that cannabis benefits chronic pain, chemotherapy-induced nausea, and spasticity associated with multiple sclerosis. A

There is also consistent, good quality evidence that cannabis causes: respiratory symptoms, motor vehicle crashes, lower birth weight, and psychosis A. There is mixed quality evidence that cannabis causes: risk of injuries in pediatric population, impaired learning, memory, and attention, depression, suicidality, social anxiety disorder, and risk for developing substance use disorder for other substances B
Patients who are pregnant or breastfeeding should be discouraged from using cannabis. C

Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is defined by DSM-5 criteria, parallel to other substance use disorders. Defining characteristics include the 4 “c’s”: cravings, compulsive use, loss of control, and continued use despite negative consequences. C

For patients struggling with CUD, the standard of care for treatment includes psychotherapy, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and motivational enhancement treatment (MET) with an added benefit of contingency management (CM). B

Currently, there are no FDA-approved pharmacotherapies available for CUD. It remains uncertain whether pharmacotherapy can improve CUD-related outcomes. For all outcomes, there is only very low- to low-certainty evidence. B

background.definition: Cannabis is a common substance of use and misuse, and consumption has been increasing in recent years. Cannabis use and cannabis use disorder are most prevalent among young adults (18-25 years old). Risk for cannabis use disorder is partly genetic and is higher in those with risk factors, including those who use cannabis more frequently or have other mental health or substance use disorders.

list.listitem: Cannabis is the most commonly used illegal psychoactive substance worldwide.
As of 2015, there were 19.8 million cases of cannabis dependence worldwide. The highest prevalence is seen in North America.

The prevalence of CUD has been increasing in the U.S. over the past two decades. From 2001- 2013, CUD prevalence increased from 1.5% to 2.9%; however, the prevalence of CUD among current U.S. cannabis users dropped from 35.6% to 30.6%. A meta-analysis using data from across the world found a prevalence of cannabis use disorder of 22% among those who have ever used cannabis - with prevalence of 13% for cannabis abuse and 13% for cannabis dependence
Both cannabis use and cannabis use disorder were more prevalent among young adults (ages 18-25) than among adolescents (ages 12-17) or adults (ages 26 and older).
Prevalence of cannabis use within the past 12 months was 10.1% for the 12-17 age group and 34.5% for the 18-25 age group.
Prevalence of cannabis use disorder within the past 12 months was 4.1% for the 12-17 age group and 13.5% for the 18-25 age group.

Cannabis is made of thousands of chemicals. The best studied include: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC): A psychostimulant, it is an agonist of CB1 receptors in the brain, spinal cord, nerves, liver, endothelium, myocardium and CB2 receptors in the immune system) CB1 or CB2 receptor activation affects the release of multiple neurotransmitters along multiple pathways including GABA, NMDA, opioid, and serotonin. Cannabidiol (CBD): Generally considered less psychoactive. Weaker affinity for CB1 and CB2 receptors. Terpenes: organic compounds that produce the unique aroma and flavor of cannabis. and may influence the intoxicating effects of cannabinoids. there are at least 100 different terpenes in the cannabis plant and each type of plant has its own unique terpenes. Flavonoids: organic compounds that produce the color and flavor of cannabis; there are at least 20 different flavonoids in the cannabis plant and each type of plant has its own unique flavonoids.

The THC percentage indicates the potency of cannabis's psychoactive effects. Samples of cannabis taken in the 1960's typically contained no more than 3-4% THC. Cannabis purchased “on the street” today has an average THC content of 16%, and in medical dispensaries, one can buy a cannabis oil that contains 88% THC.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: 50-70% of ‘liability’ to CUD is due to genetic factors, with multiple genetic associations demonstrated. There are also some morphological differences in brain structure associated with cannabis use.

There is a higher risk for developing CUD in people who use cannabis daily/weekly, and who had an earlier age of onset of cannabis use. If cannabis is used in adolescence prior to alcohol and/or tobacco, people are more likely to use cannabis heavily and develop CUD. However, the association between early age of cannabis use and development of CUD may reflect other psychiatric comorbidities and socioeconomic factors - not causality.

Risk factors for CUD include male gender, family history of substance use disorder, childhood sexual abuse, antisocial behavior, impulsivity, early-onset anxiety disorder, other illicit substance use, low educational attainment, low age at first birth, high BMI, other mental health disorders, infectious diseases, respiratory diseases.
It is unclear whether medical cannabis laws affect the prevalence of CUD.

There is an association between increased prevalence of CUD among adolescents and legalization of recreational cannabis. Adolescents in cannabis-legal states were more likely to report cannabis use in the 2017 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance Survey. Cannabis-related adolescent hospitalizations at children's hospitals have increased disproportionately following legalization of cannabis in some states.
There is growing evidence that minority stress may increase the risk of problematic cannabis use and may contribute to inequitable outcomes among those who use cannabis.
In one study of incarcerated men who identified as African American, race-related stress was associated with the number of years of cannabis use.
In a study of Black young adults, racial microaggressions were found to be a predictor of problematic alcohol and cannabis use, above the effect of trauma exposure.

One study identified intersectional minority stress as a risk factor for recent cannabis use. When specific domains of intersectional minority stress were examined, racism from SGM communities was found to be associated with greater odds of recent cannabis use.
Among a sample of Latinx 9th graders, peer-perpetuated ethnic discrimination has been described as a risk factor for cannabis use.
Perceived racial and social class discrimination may be risk factors for cannabis initiation among Black youth.

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) in 2020 gave a ‘B’ rating for screening in primary care for illicit drug use (including cannabis) in adults. B
The USPSTF gave an ‘I’ rating (insufficient evidence) for screening in primary care for illicit drug use (including cannabis) in adolescents. C

The USPSTF in 2020 gave a ‘B’ rating for screening in primary care for illicit drug use (including cannabis) in adults. Note that the favorable ‘B’ rating is driven partly by the strength of evidence around screening and treatment for opioid use disorder.
The USPSTF in 2020 gave an ‘I’ rating for screening in primary care for illicit drug use (including cannabis) in adolescents.

The CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble) is a well-validated substance use screening tool for adolescents aged 12-21. (INSERT LINK TO EE+ CALCULATOR https://www.essentialevidenceplus.com/content/rules/371)
The original CRAFFT, at a cutoff point of 2, has a sensitivity of 82.0% and specificity of 83.7% for identifying heavy cannabis use among youth.

The SB21 is another validated tool for screening for SUDs among adolescents. It asks about drug use in the past year by naming different categories of drugs. Adolescents reporting no drug/alcohol use do not require further screening. For those reporting any use over the past year, further screening is recommended.
There is poor quality evidence regarding the effectiveness of school-based prevention interventions, but skills-training interventions are likely more effective than just providing information
There is poor quality evidence about the effectiveness of non-school-based interventions to prevent or reduce drug use in those under 25 years old.
Patients should be diagnosed with CUD based on diagnostic criteria from the DSM-5 with the severity described as mild, moderate, or severe. C
A pneumonic for diagnosing CUD includes patients who meet the 4 “c’s”: cravings, compulsive use, loss of control, and continued use despite negative consequences. C
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) defines cannabis use disorder (CUD) as at least two of the following, occurring within a 12-month period:
Cannabis is often taken in larger amounts or over a longer period than was intended.
There is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control cannabis use.
A great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain cannabis, use cannabis, or recover from its effects.
Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use cannabis.
Recurrent cannabis use resulting in a failure to fulfill major role obligations at work, school, or home.
Continued cannabis use despite having persistent or recurrent social or interper­sonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of cannabis.
Important social, occupational, or recreational activities are given up or reduced be­cause of cannabis use.
Recurrent cannabis use in situations in which it is physically hazardous.
Cannabis use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by cannabis.
Tolerance (marked increase in amount; marked decrease in effect).

Withdrawal syndrome as manifested by cessation of cannabis or use of cannabis (or a closely related substance) to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms. Tolerance and withdrawal criteria alone are not sufficient to make the diagnosis (e.g., taking cannabis solely under appropriate medical supervision).
Severity of cannabis use disorder is categorized as mild (presence of 2-3 symptoms), moderate (4-5 symptoms), or severe (6 or more symptoms).
Ask about route of consumption and amount used, and assess for other substance use and substance use disorders.
Ask about previous treatments for substance use disorder with durations of successful treatment, as well as factors and circumstances contributing to disease resumption or worsening.

Ask about associated co-morbidities, including mental health disorders (common co-morbidities include mood disorders, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic distress disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), sexual abuse, domestic violence, and childhood trauma.
Evaluate for the 4 “c’s” which suggest cannabis use disorder: cravings, compulsive use, loss of control, and continued use despite negative consequences.

Assess for signs and symptoms of cannabis intoxication, including the following psychological effects : paranoia, anxiety, decreased short term memory, lethargy, impaired judgment, slow reaction time, and worsening of motor coordination affecting driving ability. Cannabis intoxication can cause physical problems: chronic bronchitis (if smoked), mild increase in blood pressure, dry mouth, dry, red eyes, and hunger (the “munchies”)

Assess for signs and symptoms of cannabis withdrawal, including having 3 or more of the following that develop after the cessation of prolonged cannabis use: irritability, anger, or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; at least one of the following physical symptoms that causes discomfort: abdominal pain, shakiness/tremors, sweating, fever, chills, or headache. Withdrawal symptoms may be present within the first 24 hours. Overall, they peak within the first week and persist up to 1 month following the last use of cannabis.

Testing for cannabis is often used by employers to ensure employee safety in preforming job-related duties (e.g., driving, flying, operating heavy machinery), in the military, among athletes, for legal/forensic reasons, and among health care workers. Keep in mind that drug tests can detect cannabis use, not cannabis use disorder, which requires further assessment.

Drug tests measure THC and/or its major metabolite. THC is highly lipophilic: it is stored in fat tissue and gradually released into the bloodstream at very low levels, permitting metabolism and eventual excretion; THC is metabolized extensively in the liver.
Cannabis can be detected in the blood for up to 7 days, hair for up to 90 days, saliva for up to 24 hours, and urine for up to 3 days (but up to 6 weeks in heavy users).

For urine drug screens, the window of detection is highly dependent on the quality of the marijuana, the individual's body fat content and metabolism. chronicity of use, the individual's state of hydration when the urine sample is collected, and the cutoff used by the laboratory.
For urine drug screens, the cut-off levels that distinguish a positive from a negative specimen are not universal and depend on the lab conducting the test.

For urine drug screens, false positives can occur with hemp-seed containing foods, low THC and CBD supplements, and proton-pump inhibitors. For confirmation, providers can order gas chromatography-mass spectrometer (GCMS) studies.

Testing positive after secondhand exposure to marijuana smoke is controversial. It is possible under extreme circumstances (i.e., riding in a closed car with others smoking cannabis) and the laboratory cut off for detection is low (20 ng/mL.)
Remind patients that cannabis is relatively safe for most people, but still carries risks. Just because states allow cannabis to be used, does not mean it is a healthy thing to do (like alcohol).
Clinicians should acknowledge that there is not great evidence around most of the harms/benefits and consider the pros/cons of cannabis use for that specific patient.

Counseling on evidence for the potential benefits and harms may include: while cannabis might improve pain, it can affect breathing, impair memory/learning attention, increase the risk for MVAs, increase the risk for mood disorders like depression/anxiety, and increase the risk of addiction to other substances.
Cannabis should be recommended against during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Remind adolescents and young adults that using cannabis at a young age can put them at higher risk for developing CUD at an older age.

For patients struggling with CUD, referring them for behavioral therapy is standard of care; While there are no FDA approved medications for treating CUD and none of them have a robust evidence base, providers can consider medication with very limited evidence: gabapentin, quetiapine, fatty acid amide hydrolase inhibitors (FAHIs), N-acteyl cysteine (NAC) for adolescents.
Provide a harm reduction message: “If you are going to use cannabis, it is best to buy it from a dispensary rather than off the street (where it could be laced with harmful drugs like fentanyl).”

Psychosocial interventions, including cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and motivational enhancement therapy (MET), with adjunctive contingency management (CM) provided over more than four sessions are considered the first-line treatment for CUD. B.
Currently, there are no FDA-approved pharmacotherapies available for CUD.
It remains uncertain whether pharmacotherapy can improve CUD-related outcomes. For all outcomes, there is only very low- to low-certainty evidence and for most there is no evidence of benefit. B.
Currently, there are no FDA-approved pharmacotherapies available for CUD. Many studies have assessed off-label use of medications FDA-approved for other indications.

It remains uncertain whether pharmacotherapy can improve CUD-related outcomes, despite a growing body of evidence examining a variety of medications. For all outcomes (abstinence, cannabis use, treatment retention, dropouts due to adverse events, serious adverse events, and withdrawal symptoms), there is only very low- to low-certainty evidence. Most pharmacotherapies for the treatment of CUD in adults and adolescents did not differ significantly from placebo in comparing efficacy and harms.

Some evidence of benefit: Compared to placebo, anticonvulsants (gabapentin 1200 mg/day), antipsychotics (quetiapine 300 mg qhs), fatty acid amide hydrolase inhibitors (PF-04457845 4 mg/day), have demonstrated decreased cannabis use and improvement in cannabis withdrawal symptoms (very low quality evidence). Glutamatergic modulators (N-acetyl cysteine 1200 mg BID) have demonstrated decreased cannabis use among adolescents and young adults (very low quality of evidence).

No evidence of benefit: Compared to placebo, SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors), SARIs (Serotonin Antagonist Reuptake inhibitors, such as trazodone and nefazodone), bupropion, mood stabilizers (including divalproex sodium, lithium), anti-anxiety medications (including buspirone), hormones (including oxytocin, progesterone), cholinesterase inhibitors (glantamine), cognitive enhancement therapies (atomoxetine), showed NO difference in outcomes related to abstinence, cannabis use, treatment retention, and/or withdrawal symptoms (very low quality of evidence).

Some evidence of harms: Compared to placebo, SNRIs (venlafaxine) demonstrated harmful effects on abstinence rates and cannabis use (very low quality of evidence). Compared to placebo, topiramate demonstrated harmful effects on treatment retention and adverse events from the medication (very low quality of evidence)

Certain cannabinoid formulations may hold promise for treatment of CUD, but results would need to be replicated in additional studies and across outcomes before being adopted in clinical practice. See .
More research is needed to identify effective pharmacological treatments for CUD.
Psychosocial interventions, including cognitive-behavioral (CBT) and motivational enhancement therapy (MET), are considered the first-line treatment for CUD.

CBT and MET have demonstrated decreased cannabis use (moderate quality of evidence), improved abstinence rates, symptoms of dependence, cannabis-related problems (low quality of evidence), and joints used per day (very low quality of evidence).

Adjunctive contingency management (CM) treatments (using abstinence-based incentives) combined with CBT or with MET + CBT produced improvements in outcomes. High-intensity interventions of more than four sessions and those delivered over longer than one month were most effective.

None of these psychotherapeutic modalities have been associated with adverse effects. Abstinence rates remain modest and decline after 9 months of treatment.
B

For adolescents, brief interventions that may or may not include motivational interviewing have a small effect in mitigating cannabis consequences (negative psychosocial repercussions, perception of cannabis use by peers, and driving under the influence).

Compared with other substances of misuse (28.3 deaths per 100,000 US population from drug intoxication), intoxication and withdrawal from cannabis is not fatal, risk of end-organ damage appears to be low, and overdose is unlikely. However, ongoing severe CUD can cause serious life disruptions and dysfunction as well as worsen other mental health conditions. A

There is an association between cannabis use disorder and many types of mental health conditions, including mood disorders, psychotic disorders, and personality disorders. However, the direction of causality is not clear, e.g., these disorders may make someone more likely to use cannabis or cannabis may increase the risk of these disorders. A

Cannabis use disorder is associated with higher rates of major depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar 1, bipolar 2, and anxiety disorders. It is unclear whether there are causal relationships between CUD and these other conditions.Among people with bipolar disorder, there is a weak association between CUD and suicide attempts.
Cannabis use raises risk for new-onset psychosis and worsens prognosis in existing psychotic disorders, and more frequent and/or higher-potency THC use elevates risk in a dose-response manner. A
Cannabis use disorder is also associated with personality disorders - most strongly borderline or antisocial personality disorder. A
Cannabis use has effects on neuropsychological functioning:
While past studies demonstrated a drop in IQ in adolescents who chronically used cannabis, more recent studies refuted the results.

More studies including periodic brain imaging would help clarify what effects cannabis consumption might have on brain development, neurocognitive function and mental illness The ABCD study, a prospective study that aims to follow 10,000 children as they transition into adulthood and is ongoing.
Multiple other studies have reported an association between adolescent-onset cannabis use and impairment in several cognitive domains, including learning, memory, and executive function.
Cannabis use in adolescents is associated with increased risk of psychiatric conditions:

There is a well-described association between cannabis use and schizophrenia. A large Swedish cohort study reported a six-fold increased risk of developing schizophrenia among those with heavy cannabis use at age 18.

In a registry study comparing patients with cannabis-induced psychosis to matched controls, those with cannabis-induced psychosis were significantly more likely to develop schizophrenia (HR 101.7, p < 0.001) and bipolar disorder (HR 32.5, p < 0.001). 47.4% of patients with cannabis-induced psychosis converted to either schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. The risk of converting from any substance-induced psychosis to schizophrenia was greatest when the substance-induced psychosis occurred between ages 16 and 25. There was no age-related association for conversion to bipolar disorder.
Cannabis use in young adulthood is associated with increased risk of developing depression and suicide ideation.
Cannabis may be the most commonly used illicit drug in pregnancy.
Self-reported prevalence of cannabis use during pregnancy tends to range from 2-5%, but may be higher among young, urban, and socioeconomically disadvantaged populations.
In one study, 18.1% of pregnant people who reported cannabis use in the past year met criteria for CUD.

listitem.strong: Effects on the mother and developing fetus

list.listitem: There is substantial evidence of the statistical association between maternal cannabis smoking and lower birth weight of offspring. There may be a dose-response relationship.

There is limited evidence of the statistical association between maternal cannabis smoking and pregnancy complications for the mother AND admission of the infant to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).

There is insufficient evidence to support or refute a statistical association between maternal cannabis smoking and later outcomes in the offspring (IDS, cognitive/academic achievements, and later substance use).
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends complete cessation of cannabis use during pregnancy.
To avoid exposing their infants to cannabis, it is recommended that breastfeeding mothers not consume cannabis. This is in line with the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine's recommendations.

feature.caption: Impact of cannabinoid formulation; overall quality of evidence is low

tr.td: Compared with placebo, cannabinoids with low THC to CBD ratio in low-dose formulation have demonstrated improvements in abstinence rates, cannabis use, and withdrawal symptoms, and in high-dose formulation have demonstrated improvements in withdrawal symptoms.
Compared with placebo, cannabinoids with high THC to CBD ratio have demonstrated mixed/conflicting results around retention in treatment and withdrawal symptoms.
Compared with placebo, cannabinoids with comparable THC to CBD ratio have demonstrated improvements in absence rates and mixed/conflicting results around cannabis use and retention in treatment.
